fields.title: API as a Contract
fields.keyTakeaway: An API is an agreement on what can be asked, and a PM must distinguish between "no data" and "data not provided" because it determines whether a feature is impossible or requires negotiation.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: What exactly does an engineer mean when they say "they don't have that in the API", and why is it not the same as "they don't have that data"?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: The difference between "no data" and "data exists but isn't served" determines whether a feature is possible at all or if it's a matter of negotiating with a partner. A PM who does not distinguish these cases either turns down what is possible or promises the impossible.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: [[api|API]] is a set of operations that one system provides to another. It is a [[contract|contract]]: both parties agreed on what can be asked, in what format, and what will come in response.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: An operation is described by four things.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **[[endpoint|Endpoint]]** — the address of the operation. `/v1/orders/4471` — "order with this number".
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **[[http-method|Method]]** — what we are doing. [[term-2|`GET`]] to retrieve, `POST` to create, `PATCH` to modify, `DELETE` to remove. The distinction is not a formality: `GET` is safe and repeatable, `POST` creates and if repeated will create a second one.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Input** — [[query-parameter|parameters]] in the address (filters, page) and [[request-body|body]] for creation and modification. Plus [[header|headers]]: [[access-token|access token]], version, format.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: The product essence of the contract is that **it restricts both parties.** The provider cannot silently remove a field — they have consumers. We cannot request something that is not in the contract, even if they have the data.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: Hence three different situations that sound identical:
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: *No data.* The provider does not collect it. Cannot be solved by anything other than changing their product.
fields.sections/2/blocks/9/text: *Data exists, not exposed in the API.* Solved by a request for modification. The timeline depends on their priorities, but this is a negotiation.
fields.sections/2/blocks/10/text: *Data exists and is exposed, but inconveniently.* Requires five requests instead of one, or lacks a filter. Solved on our side at the cost of complexity.
fields.sections/2/blocks/11/text: The question to the engineer is formulated accordingly: not "can this be done", but "is this missing from the contract or do they not have it at all".
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Payment provider.* Need to show the last four digits of the card in history. The field is not in the contract. Requested — it turned out the data exists, exposed within three weeks per their schedule. Situation two.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *Delivery service.* Need to show the courier on the map. Data on the courier's location is not collected by them at all — only statuses "accepted", "in transit", "delivered". Situation one, feature closed.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Catalog supplier.* Need products by category. The method exists, but there is no category filter — only an export of the entire catalog at once, 40 thousand items. Situation three: fetch everything once a day and filter on our side.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: The contract describes the shape, but not the meaning. The `status` field can be named the same and mean different things in different versions. Discrepancy of meaning with matching shape is the most unpleasant type of failure because nothing crashes.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: API is an agreement on what can be asked, and a PM must distinguish between "no data" and "data not provided" because it determines whether a feature is impossible or requires negotiation.
